newsitem.title: FRANCE: Algerians to vote on draft constitution.
newsitem.headline: Algerians to vote on draft constitution.

text.p: Algerians go to the polls on Thursday amid tight security to vote on a draft constitution that would ban Moslem fundamentalists from seeking power.
Algerian authorities, fearing violence after guerrillas said they will disrupt the vote, have shut schools and turned them into heavily fortified polling stations ringed by soldiers, residents said.
"Schools have been closed since three days and security forces and soldiers were put up there," said Fatiha, a housewife in Algiers's Bab el Oued, a stronghold of Moslem militants.
The government ordered a week-long closure of big markets in the cities, where thousands of army paratroopers, police and paramilitary forces have deployed along the roads.
The authorities also announced a nationwide ban on truck traffic throughout the country starting on Thursday to protect against car bomb attacks by the rebels.
"The government does not want to give any chance to armed groups," said an Algiers-based western diplomat.
More than 1,400 people have been killing in bombings in the past two years, according to a government-appointed human rights group report.
Five people died last Sunday when a car bomb exploded in downtown Blida, 50 km (30 miles) south of Algiers. Blida is the site of a main military headquarters.

The militant Armed Islamic Group (GIA) -- the most feared of the armed Moslem movements -- has warned people not to vote, saying its guerrillas will "strike the neck" of anyone who leave his home on referendum day.
Moslem rebels earlier this week chased off telecommunications workers who wanted to fix phone lines at a polling station in the Casbah, Algiers city old heart.
"They returned the next day escorted by security forces," said a resident of the area.

Government officials and their political backers, who hope to see a high turnout of the 16.4 million potential voters to boost support for President Liamine Zeroual, made last hour calls that people endorse the constitutional reforms.
"Don't forget the years of hell and sacrifices," said Prime Minister Ahmed Ouyahia in a campaign rally, referring to the country's five-year-old civil strife.
More than 60,000 people have been killed in Algeria's violence since early 1992 when the authorities scrapped a general elections that radical Islamists were poised to win.
Opposition leaders continued their campaign against the referendum, hoping for a low turnout to embarrass the government.
Analysts have said that Algerian voters, who turned out in large numbers in last year's poll to return Zeroual to power as president, seem less enthusiastic to vote in the constitutional referendum.

Many Algerians, rather than asking questions about the proposed constitution banning Moslem fundamentalists, have assailed government ministers at campaign rallies over corruption, political violence and economic hardship.

"The new constitution provides weapons to the president to control, manipulate and dissolve the political parties. The authorities can obviously find any pretext to ban our party," said Socialist Forces Front chief Hocine Ait Ahmed.
Editors of the country's independent newspapers on Wednesday denounced the government for tightening control on the media ahead of the referendum.

"The television (campaign) coverage reminded Algerians of the dark years and symbols of the sole ruling party," said the outlawed Islamic Salvation Front in a comment in its clandestine paper el Ribat.
The proposed constitution would replace the 1989 constitution that ended a three decades of monopoly rule by the National Liberation Front party.
